proof.criterion: The architect's first check: the document-write row passes 20 of 20 runs with --retries=0, keeping every failing run's trace (A1's write half, the 1 s bound unchanged).
proof.surface: The Dispatch API's document write (POST of an issue artifact) against the real Go server and Postgres, driven by the row the suite ships, on this pod's harness.
proof.command: export LEGION_ROLE=tester && source /legion/harness/env.sh && cd packages/dispatch && bun run build:web && for n in $(seq 1 20); do rm -rf e2e/test-results; PLAYWRIGHT_JSON_OUTPUT_NAME=$TMPDIR/r4-write2/$n.json bun e2e/run.ts -- bunx playwright test --config e2e/playwright.config.ts heavy-bodies.e2e.ts --project=chromium --retries=0 --reporter=json -g 'a document write of each heavy body' > $TMPDIR/r4-write2/$n.out; cp -r e2e/test-results $TMPDIR/r4-write2/$n/ 2>/dev/null; done
proof.observed: 20 of 20 passed, no failing run and so no trace to keep. The parse-bound shape's warming write, which the row records rather than bounds, read 789-1,312 ms across the twenty. An earlier series of twenty, started while my own `bun run build:web` was still finishing on this two-core pod, gave 19 of 20 with its one failure at 1,272 ms for the 8,000-item list; I am recording that as my own contention rather than the change's, which is why the series above was run with nothing else of mine running, and it is also the measurement the architect's bar names.
proof.negativeControl: The row refuses four of its eight bodies - 100 items nested by indentation, 15,999 markers on one line, a callout opener holding 15,000 brackets - and each answered 400 with code INVALID_MARKDOWN in every one of the twenty runs; a run where the nesting bound was not wired would store them and fail the row. The round-3 failures of this same row (1,025 ms and 1,504 ms, traces kept then) are the control that it can fail.

proof.criterion: The architect's recorded risk: twenty back-to-back warm writes of the 8,000-item list do not all stay under 800 ms, and the cause is each write's queued settlement landing on the writes after it.
proof.surface: The same API write, twenty times in one warmed server process, with no browser work in the loop, then the same twenty four seconds apart.
proof.command: A throwaway spec (deleted after the run) that calls createIssueArtifact twenty times on one issue and records each write's milliseconds, then repeats it with a 4,000 ms gap.
proof.observed: Back to back: 656, 436, 507, 402, 389, 472, 614, 916, 938, 795, 732, 752, 567, 429, 692, 515, 699, 836, 654, 748 ms - 3 of 20 at or over 800 ms, median 656, worst 938. Four seconds apart: 826, 346, 779, 384, 547, 578, 704, 475, 386, 377, 369, 776, 312, 626, 625, 309, 730, 308, 306, 620 ms - 1 of 20 at or over 800, median 547, worst 826. So the implementer's account holds, and the shape of it is the risk the architect accepted. Two things worth keeping beside it: every one of those forty writes is under the 1 s bound the row holds, where round 3's same measurement at the old code had two of ten over it (488-1,144 ms); and the climb is not monotonic here, so what the gap buys is the median (656 to 547) more than the worst.
proof.negativeControl: The spaced series is the control for the back-to-back one: same body, same process, same code, and the only difference is the four seconds, which moves 3 of 20 over the bar down to 1 of 20 - so what the numbers show is the settlement's load and not the parse.
